However, this percentage remains significantly above the ~32% average seen in the 20 years before the 2020 pandemic.

To put this into perspective, during the 2012-2019 period, this figure never materially exceeded 30%.

The fight against inflation is far from over.

History suggests volatility is ahead.

Since 1928, the S&P 500 has fallen ~55% of the time in September, making it the only month of the year when negative returns have occurred more often than positive returns.

Over this period, the average return of the index has been -1.1%, with an average drawdown of -4.7%.

Furthermore, the best September recorded a +14.4% gain, while the worst saw a -29.9% decline.

The weakness has historically been concentrated later in the month, with the second half of September averaging a -0.9% return, making it the weakest 2-week period of the year.

By comparison, the first half has seen an average decline of -0.2%.

BREAKING: The 60+ day delinquency rate on US subprime auto loans is up to ~5.2%, the highest on record.

This figure has more than doubled over the last 4 years.

Serious delinquency rates on subprime auto loans are now ~1.7 percentage points above their 2008 Financial Crisis peak.

At the same time, 60+ day delinquencies on prime auto loans are up to ~0.4%, near their highest since 2011.

Meanwhile, total US auto debt surged +$28 billion in Q2 2026, to a record $1.71 trillion.

Americans are falling behind on their car payments at a historic rate.

China is increasingly relying on Russian oil amid the Iran War.

China's imports of Russian oil rose by ~200,000 barrels per day in August, to ~1.6 million barrels per day, their highest since March.

This marks the 3rd consecutive monthly increase, bringing the cumulative gain over that stretch to ~500,000 barrels per day.

This is now above the levels seen in the last 4 months of 2025.

By comparison, China imported ~2.0 million barrels per day from Russia in February.

This comes as Middle East oil supplies have become more constrained and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted, prompting Chinese refiners to turn increasingly to Russian crude.
